blocks.text: Isaiah presents Assyria as an instrument of judgment while also holding its king accountable for arrogant, destructive ambition (vv. 5–19). Read alongside the chapter’s call for the remnant to cease relying on the one who struck them and instead to rely on the Holy One of Israel (vv. 20–23), this makes political power and trust inseparable concerns. This reading is disputed, but it highlights the chapter’s refusal to treat imperial military strength as the final authority.

Romans later cites Isaiah’s language about a remnant returning after speaking of a call from both Jews and gentiles and alongside Hosea’s reversal of “not my people.” This later rereading is disputed; it should not be taken to transfer Isaiah’s language of Israel’s restoration away from Israel.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly aligns with the Masoretic tradition while also preserving thousands of spelling and substantive differences; other Qumran Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings show that Isaiah was actively copied and interpreted. These textual details concern the book’s wider transmission rather than a direct claim about Isaiah 10 alone.
